extracted.intended_audience: judge advocates, military legal officers, and practitioners handling courts-martial
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing service of process, witness attendance and fees, privileges, admissibility and weight of evidence, authentication of official records, and procedures in trials by courts-martial. Applicable guidance for judge advocates and military courts on handling testimony, subpoenas, attachments, confessions, accused testimony, and documentary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of summons — who may serve
rubrics_metrics.description: A summons may legally be served either by a military or a civil person, but will in general preferably be served by an officer or noncommissioned officer of the Army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judge advocate or commanding officer is not authorized to employ a U.S. marshal or other civil official so as to commit the United States to payment of fees; however, in cases where employing a civilian is the most economical and effectual means, the Secretary of War has in some cases ratified reasonable charges payable from Army contingencies (citations given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees for service of subpoenas — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no fee or compensation established or authorized to be paid by statute or regulation for the service of subpoenas for the attendance of witnesses before military courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither a commanding officer nor a judge advocate is authorized to employ a civilian for such service or to commit the United States to payment of any compensation to such a person; exceptions have been made where employment of a civilian was the most economical and effectual course and so ratified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of subpoenas abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: Subpoenas for witnesses residing in foreign territory should be transmitted through the Department of State for service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness cannot unilaterally excuse himself
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness can have no authority to discharge or relieve himself from attendance on the ground that the testimony desired of him is immaterial, or for any other reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is for the court to judge materiality; unless the court determines a witness to be incompetent or testimony inadmissible, he should remain and stand his examination until informed by the court or judge advocate that his attendance is no longer required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege against self-incrimination is personal
rubrics_metrics.description: The common-law privilege to refuse to respond to a question that may criminate is a personal one which the witness may exercise or waive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not for the judge advocate or accused to object or to check the witness; the court may advise an ignorant witness of the right. If the court decides the question is not incriminating and the witness still refuses, the witness may be liable to charges under article 62.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness privilege cannot be exercised by others on behalf of witness
rubrics_metrics.description: The privilege to decline answering incriminating questions belongs to the witness only; a court ordering a witness to testify to facts that would incriminate him is erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: trial of a cadet where the court required another cadet to testify to incriminating facts — held erroneous; witness should be instructed of rights if ignorant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge advocate's duty regarding incriminating questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The ninety‑th article of war charges the judge advocate with the duty of objecting, during the progress of a trial, 'to any question to the prisoner the answer to which might tend to criminate himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compulsion implies force or duress; ordinary lawful physical examinations by medical officers may produce observations that are admissible testimony and do not amount to compelled incrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: entitlement to witness fees without formal subpoena
rubrics_metrics.description: To entitle a witness to the payment of fees, it is not absolutely essential that he should produce a formal summons or subpoena; it will generally be sufficient if he has duly attended in compliance with a verbal or informal written request from the judge advocate, or at the instance of the accused if acquiesced in by the judge advocate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person cannot claim witness fees merely by appearing on his own responsibility and not at the instance of either party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for loss of time/business not compensable
rubrics_metrics.description: A party who attended as a witness and claimed indemnification for loss of time and injury to his business beyond regular per diem compensation cannot be allowed such a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such losses are disadvantages citizens must bear in discharge of public obligations; no remedy provided by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation for expert witnesses (handwriting, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compensation allowed by the Secretary of War for witnesses summoned as experts (e.g., in handwriting) before courts‑martial is payable out of the annual appropriation for compensation of witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When necessity for an expert arises, necessity must be shown by resolution of the court and Secretary's authority secured in advance (citation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation and Secretary's authority to fix witness fees
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual appropriation by Congress for compensation of witnesses attending courts‑martial was based on understanding that compensation, not prescribed by statute, was left to be fixed by the Secretary of War and published in Army Regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 848 R.S. (witness fees for federal civil courts) has no application to courts‑martial; appropriation regarded as made in recognition of rates established by regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees for foreign civilian witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees to foreign civilian witnesses before courts‑martial are the same as those allowed by United States courts at the place of trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement voucher for lost witness voucher
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the voucher of a witness has been lost, a new voucher may be issued by the judge advocate upon satisfactory showing of such loss, supported by affidavit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new voucher should be noted to indicate its character and forwarded to the Paymaster General for settlement (C. 21516, May 8, 1907).

rubrics_metrics.name: Police and postmasters as 'civilians in employ of the Government'
rubrics_metrics.description: Policemen of the District of Columbia and postmasters are 'civilians in the employ of the Government' as contemplated by paragraph 1006, Army Regulations (1910).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited decisions classify such persons as civilians for purposes of witness/compensation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachment to compel attendance requires formal summons
rubrics_metrics.description: To authorize resort to an attachment there must have been a formal summons, duly issued and served upon the witness, and not complied with.

rubrics_metrics.name: No attachment to compel deposition before commissioner
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute cannot properly be construed as authorizing the issue of an attachment to compel a witness to attend before a commissioner or other person and give his deposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may execute an attachment in military cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge advocate cannot properly direct an attachment to a U.S. marshal or other civil official; some military officer or person should be designated or detailed for the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In executing an attachment, necessary force may be employed (citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection from arrest while attending court-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: The common-law principle protecting a witness from arrest should, in general, be applied to military cases; arrest should be avoided while attending court‑martial as witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an arrest would be an irregularity only and would not affect the validity of subsequent proceedings against the party arrested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts‑martial to follow civil rules of evidence but with indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts‑martial should in general follow, so far as apposite, the rules of evidence observed by the civil courts, especially U.S. criminal courts, but are not bound by statute and may apply rules with more indulgence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They may allow more latitude in introduction, examination and cross‑examination of witnesses than civil tribunals; avoid overtechnicality because persons tried by courts‑martial are often not versed in legal practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that public officers perform duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The law presumes that public officers duly perform their official functions, and this presumption continues until the contrary is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of evidence apply irrespective of rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of evidence should be applied by military courts irrespective of the rank of the person to be affected; witnesses for the prosecution may be cross‑examined about animosity or prior contradictory statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such questioning is admissible by established law of evidence and does not imply disrespect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plea of guilty to lesser included offense (absence without leave)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier charged with desertion pleads guilty of absence without leave but not guilty of desertion, the judge advocate bears the burden of proving animus non revertendi (intent to not return) — the gist of desertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although long absence may furnish presumption of intent, evidence (even slight) should be introduced to support a finding (C. 17313, Dec 23, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Official communications privileged
rubrics_metrics.description: Official communications between heads of Government departments and their subordinate officers are privileged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privilege necessary to permit effective administration of public affairs (P. 52, 344, Mar., 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency of public enemies as witnesses and caution on corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Being a public enemy or giving aid to the enemy does not affect competency of testimony before a court‑martial, but their statements in wartime (for enemy/favoring enemy or against Federal officers) should be received with caution unless corroborated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: numerous decisions showing caution analogous to accomplice testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confessions must be free and voluntary
rubrics_metrics.description: A confession is competent evidence when free and voluntary; a confession made through influence of fear or hope of favor is not admissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: confession induced by police promise of opportunity to escape held inadmissible; confessions by private soldiers to officers should be received with caution given military relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpus delicti requirement before admission of confession
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier voluntarily confesses absence without authority, before admission of the confession the corpus delicti (unauthorized absence) must be proved; intent remains for court to determine after considering all evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of testimony that accused 'was drunk'
rubrics_metrics.description: On trials for drunkenness or drunken conduct it is admissible to ask a witness directly if the accused 'was drunk' or to have a witness state that the accused 'was drunk' on the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statements are treated as matters of observation (palpable to persons in general) rather than expert opinion and are proper for any witness (citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drunkenness not an excuse but relevant to intent/grade of offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Drunkenness is no excuse for crime and voluntary drunkenness does not extenuate, yet the existence and measure of drunkenness may be proper evidence to determine species or grade of crime (e.g., malice, intent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine specific intent such as animus furandi or malice for degrees of homicide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perjury proof requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To sustain a charge of perjury, the evidence of two witnesses or of one witness with strong corroborating circumstances is necessary to prove the falsity of witness statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeaching testimony as material for perjury
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony consisting of answers to questions going to the credit of a particular witness or other witnesses he corroborated is 'material to the issue' in a perjury context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refreshing memory outside courtroom irregular
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting a witness to temporarily suspend testimony and leave the courtroom to refresh his memory as to certain dates is irregular; further testimony about those dates is inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such procedure prevents the court and accused from knowing by what means memory was refreshed and may have involved outside oral statements (P. 24, 284, May, 1888).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good character evidence admissible post-conviction for punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of the good character, record, and services of the accused as an officer or soldier is admissible in all military cases upon conviction to affect measure of punishment or recommendation for clemency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution may offer counter testimony, but cannot attack character unless the accused first introduces such evidence and thus puts it in issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutor may introduce sanity evidence with court consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge advocate may, with the consent of the court, introduce evidence as to the sanity of the accused for the purpose of removing any doubt on that subject that may exist in the mind of any member of the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no doubt exists in any member's mind, such evidence need not be introduced (C. 2994, Aug. 30, 1897).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadmissibility of prior court-martial record to show victim's character
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence offered to exhibit the character and disposition of the victim by introducing a prior general court‑martial order and findings against that victim is wholly inadmissible for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: attempt to show victim's alleged prior dishonest and unbecoming conduct via old court‑martial order — held inadmissible (P. 65, 270, June, 1894).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior trial testimony not admissible without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Except by consent of the opposite party, testimony contained in the record of a previous trial of the same or a similar case cannot properly be received in evidence on a trial by court‑martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony from previous hearings, if desired, must be offered de novo and as original matter unless otherwise specially stipulated or provided by the one hundred and twenty‑first article of war (R. 19, 41, 1860; 27, 318, Oct., 1868).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accused may introduce extenuating facts to reduce punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: On trials by court‑martial, the accused may put in evidence any facts going to extenuate the offense and reduce the punishment (e.g., prolonged pretrial confinement, prior punishment, acts sanctioned by superior authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence admissible to mitigate sentence or influence recommendation (R. 28, 104, Aug., 1868).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accused's testimony — right and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: An accused's testimony is competent only when he requests to be admitted to testify (act of Mar. 16, 1878); such testimony is subject to ordinary rules governing admissibility and cross‑examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An accused cannot be compelled to testify or to incriminate himself as to offenses he has not testified about; if he takes the stand he must testify to all facts within his knowledge relevant to the case, and on cross‑examination cannot be compelled to testify to matters not brought out on direct examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of evidence not dependent on number of witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The weight of evidence does not depend upon the number of witnesses; a single credible witness may outweigh several less satisfactory witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's assessment of credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When evidence is conflicting, the court must determine the measure of credibility to be attached to several witnesses and may consider appearance, deportment, and manner of testifying, especially under cross‑examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muster rolls and documentary evidence as primary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Muster‑in rolls are primary evidence of dates of muster in and muster‑out rolls of dates of muster out; official records are high class evidence as to facts recorded for the special objects for which they are kept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They may not have the same weight for other incidental facts recorded; citations provided (C. 9421, Dec., 1900).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication of official copies for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: War Dept. Orders (May 15, 1894) provide official copies be authenticated by an impressed seal for administrative business; such authentication was intended for administrative use, not as evidence before courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For courts, copies must be authenticated as required by section 882 R.S.; in practice many bureau‑stamped copies have been admitted before courts‑martial in absence of objection, and Secretary could legally regulate admissibility before courts‑martial (C. 8471, June, 1900 and other citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original enlistment and medical records admissible; sealed copies equal
rubrics_metrics.description: The enlistment paper, physical examination paper, and outline card are original writings made by officers in performance of duty and are competent evidence; copies authenticated under the seal of the War Department (section 882 R.S.) are equally admissible with originals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copies of courts-martial records under War Dept. seal admissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of records of courts‑martial authenticated under the seal of the War Department as provided by section 882 R.S. are admissible in evidence equally with the originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 54, 77, July, 1887; practice noted where bureau stamps used and admitted absent objection.
